title: Geometric Factual Recall in Transformers
claim: Learned embeddings need only logarithmic dimension as the number of facts grows, while frozen embeddings need polynomial or linear growth.
layout: 2 side-by-side log-log line plots, shared axes, fit equations in legends
description: Two side-by-side line plots on log-log axes. The title of each is 'Capacity scaling: d_min vs N (R=8, acc threshold=0.95)'. The x-axis is N, the number of subjects, from 2^7 to 2^15. The y-axis is d_min, the minimum embedding dimension needed to reach the accuracy threshold. Each panel has a blue circle curve for trainable embeddings and a red square curve for frozen embeddings. Dashed fit lines sit behind the curves. The legends give the fits. Trainable embeddings follow a log2 N fit. Frozen embeddings follow a square-root fit with exponent 0.55 in panel (a) and a linear fit with exponent 1.08 in panel (b). The red curve climbs far above the nearly flat blue one. Panel captions are '(a) MLP width = 4d' and '(b) MLP width = 64'. The eye goes first to the widening gap between the red and blue curves.
caption: Scaling behavior of factual recall with learned or frozen embeddings.
abstract: How do transformer language models memorize factual associations? A common account views internal weight matrices as an associative memory. That account requires parameter counts that scale linearly with the number of facts. We develop a theoretical and empirical account of an alternative, \emph{geometric} form of memorization in which learned embeddings encode relational structure directly, and the MLP plays a qualitatively different role. In a controlled setting where a single-layer transformer memorizes random bijections from subjects to a shared attribute set, we prove that a logarithmic embedding dimension is sufficient. Subject embeddings encode \emph{linear superpositions} of their associated attribute vectors, and a small MLP acts as a relation-conditioned selector that extracts the relevant attribute from the embedding. We extend these results to the multi-hop setting---chains of relational queries such as ``Who is the mother of the wife of $x$?''---and provide constructions with and without chain-of-thought that exhibit a provable capacity--depth tradeoff, complemented by a matching information-theoretic lower bound. Empirically, gradient descent discovers solutions with the predicted structure. Causal experiments support the proposed mechanism: when subject embeddings are appropriately re-initialized, the frozen MLP transfers zero-shot to entirely new bijections, showing it has learned a generic selection mechanism rather than functioning as a key-value memory.
